title: Websites, Servers, and Addresses
summary: Learn what a website is made of, what a server does, and what each piece of a web address means, then run a server on your own computer.
intro: A page that won't load, a picture that doesn't show, a link that says page not found: each of these goes wrong somewhere between the address you typed and the files that came back. To build websites, and to fix them when they break, you need to know what happens in between. This lesson starts at the very beginning: what a website is made of, where it lives, what a server is, how a browser asks one for a page, and what each piece of a web address means. In the last part, you'll run a small server on your own computer and watch your browser ask it for pages.

steps.title: What a website is made of
steps.body:
Building a website starts with knowing what one is, and the answer is less mysterious than it looks: a website is a set of files in folders, kept on a computer somewhere. Everything else in this course builds on that picture. ## Files and folders A **file** is one named piece of stored information: a photo, a song, a document. A **folder** holds files, and other folders too, so related things stay together. Your own computer stores everything this way, and so does every computer that holds a website. A folder is also called a **directory**, and you'll see both words. A file's name usually ends in a dot and a few letters, like `.jpg` or `.pdf`. That ending is the **extension**, and it tells programs what kind of file it is. On a website you'll meet these most: | Extension | What the file holds | |---|---| | `.html` | a page: its text, and what each piece of text is | | `.css` | styles: colors, sizes, and layout | | `.js` | JavaScript: what the page does | | `.png`, `.jpg`, `.svg` | pictures | ## A page is a text file An `.html` file is plain text, the kind you could type in any text editor. Here's a whole page, saved as `about.html`: ```html About me

About me

I am learning how the web works.

``` The words in angle brackets are **tags**: they tell the browser what each piece of text is. `` holds the name shown on the browser tab, `<h1>` is the page's main heading, and `<p>` is a paragraph. Open this file in a browser and you'd see About me in big letters, with one line under it. The HTML lessons explain every line, but the idea to keep for now is simple: the browser reads text and draws a page from it. ## A website is a folder of files A whole website is a folder of files like that one: ```text my-site/ index.html about.html style.css images/ logo.png ``` `index.html` is the home page, the one you see first. Every website follows that naming habit, and the part about paths shows why. One page often needs several files: the HTML, a CSS file with its styles, called a **stylesheet**, and the pictures it shows. The browser fetches each file on its own and puts the page together. ## Bytes Computers store everything as numbers, and the basic unit is the **byte**. In plain English text, one letter is one byte, so `about.html` above is 98 bytes: its letters, spaces, and line breaks. A thousand bytes make a kilobyte (KB), and a million make a megabyte (MB), about the size of a photo. When people say a server sends a file's bytes, they mean its contents, exactly as they're stored. ## Somewhere else, always on A website's folder doesn't live on your computer. It lives on a computer somewhere else that stays switched on and connected all the time, so anyone can reach it at any hour. To show you a page, your browser has to get copies of those files onto your computer. Making that trip possible is what the web is for. ## The internet and the web These two words get mixed up, and the difference helps. The **internet** is the network: the cables, Wi-Fi, and phone signals that connect computers all over the world, like a road network connecting every town. The **web** is one thing that travels on it: pages, and the files that make them. Email and video calls use the internet too, but they aren't the web, the same way the roads carry buses and trucks as well as the mail. ## Websites and web apps Some sites mostly show you things to read, like a news story or a recipe. Others are tools you use, like a map you can drag, an email inbox, or a document you edit with friends. People call the second kind **web apps**. Both are made of the same kinds of files: the more a site's JavaScript does after the page appears, the more it behaves like an app. This course teaches you to build both.

steps.title: Servers, requests, and responses
steps.body:
Every page you open is a short conversation between two programs: one asks, and the other answers. Once you know who says what, messages like 404 Not Found stop being mysterious, because they're simply one side of that conversation.

## The server

The computer that holds a website runs a program whose whole job is to wait for other computers to ask for files, and send the files back. That program is a **server**. People use the same word for the computer it runs on, so a company's servers can mean either. One server can answer thousands of people at the same moment, which is how one site can serve the whole world.

## The client

The program that does the asking is the **client**. Your browser is a client. So is the app on your phone that loads the weather, and so is `curl`, a program you type in a terminal, which you'll use later in this lesson. The client always starts the conversation: a server never reaches out to you on its own. It waits, answers, and waits again.

## Request and response

Think of a shop counter. You walk up and ask for something, the person behind the counter fetches it from the back, and they hand it over, or tell you they don't have it. The web works the same way, one item at a time.

- A **request** is the message the client sends: please give me this one thing. It names the thing by its **path**, like `/about.html`, which says which file to fetch. The next two parts explain paths in full.
- A **response** is the message the server sends back. It starts with a **status code**, a number that says how it went, and then comes the thing itself.

```diagram client-server
One request goes out, and one response comes back.
```

In the diagram, the browser sends `GET /about.html`. **GET** is the request's way of saying give me, and it's the most common kind of request. The server finds `about.html` among its files and answers `200 OK`, which means here it is, followed by the file's contents. When the server has no such file, it answers `404 Not Found` instead. You've probably seen that one. It's a real answer, not a broken connection: the server heard you fine, and it's telling you there's nothing at that address.

A page with a stylesheet and two pictures takes four requests: one for the HTML, then one for each file the HTML mentions. The browser sends them as it reads the page, and puts the page together as the answers come in.

## The same file, or one made for you

A server can make its answer in two ways.

- A **static** response is a file that already exists, sent as it is. Everyone who asks for `/about.html` gets the same bytes. Think of a printed menu: every customer gets the same one.
- A **generated** response is made by a program at the moment you ask. Your email inbox, your search results, and your bank balance are generated, since they're different for every person and every minute. Think of a receipt, printed for your order alone.

Most sites mix the two. Pictures, stylesheets, and JavaScript files are usually static, and the parts that change for each person are generated.

## Frontend and backend

The two sides of the conversation give web development its two halves.

- The **frontend** is everything that runs in the browser: the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript the server sends, and what that code does on your screen.
- The **backend** is everything that runs on the server: the programs that answer requests, and the stored information they use, like accounts and orders.

The two halves only ever talk through requests and responses. Code on the frontend can't reach into the server and read its files, and the server can't touch your screen. This course teaches the frontend, and Hack University's backend courses teach the other half.

steps.title: The address in the bar, piece by piece
steps.body:
The address you type is the request's instructions: how to ask, which computer to ask, and what to ask it for. Every link you write as a web developer is an address, and plenty of bugs come down to one wrong piece of one, so it pays to know each piece by name.

## A URL

A web address is called a **URL**, short for Uniform Resource Locator, a formal way of saying where to find something. Like a postal address, it holds several pieces, each narrowing things down, from which computer to ask all the way to one spot on one page. Here's a URL with every common piece:

```diagram address-parts
Each piece has a job, and the fragment never leaves your browser.
```

## The pieces, left to right

- The **scheme**, `https`, says which rules the browser and the server will use to talk. A set of agreed rules like that is called a **protocol**. `https` and `http` are the web's two, and the `s` stands for secure: the conversation is scrambled so nobody in between can read it. The next lesson explains how. The `://` after it only separates it from the rest.
- The **host**, `shop.example.com`, names the computer to ask. It's also called the **domain name**. Read it from the right: `com` is the large group it belongs to (others are `org`, `net`, and country groups like `uk`), `example` is the name someone registered in that group, and `shop` is one part of their site with its own name. The next lesson shows how the browser turns that name into a real computer.
- The **path**, `/search`, says what you want from that computer. It always starts with `/`. On a site made of files, it's the place of a file in the site's folder, like `/about.html`. The next part is all about paths.
- The **query string**, `?q=red+shoes`, carries extra details. It starts with `?`, and each detail is a name and a value joined by `=`. Here the name is `q`, short for query, and the value is the search words, red shoes. Several details are joined with `&`, like `?q=red+shoes&size=9`. Searches, filters, and page numbers usually go here.
- The **fragment**, `#reviews`, points at one spot inside the page, like a heading partway down. It starts with `#`, and once the page has loaded, the browser scrolls there.

## What the server sees

When the browser sends its request, it sends the path and the query string, and nothing after the `#`. The fragment stays in your browser, because it's only about where to scroll in a page you already have. That's why a link that changes only the fragment scrolls the page without loading it again.

## A number you'll sometimes see

Some addresses have a colon and a number after the host, like `localhost:3000`, the address you open Hack University at. That number is a **port**, and it picks one program on the computer. It's usually left out, and then the browser uses a standard number. The next lesson explains ports, and `localhost` too.

## What the address bar hides

Browsers tidy up the address bar. Many hide `https://`, and some show only the host until you click in the bar. When you need the whole address, click in the address bar and every piece appears. Typing only `example.com` works because the browser adds `https://` for you, and an address with no path means the home page, `/`.

## Characters with a job

Some characters have a job in a URL: `/` separates the path, `?` starts the query string, `&` and `=` split it up, and `#` starts the fragment. A space isn't allowed at all. To put one of these characters inside a value, it's written as a `%` followed by a code, which is called **percent-encoding**. A space becomes `%20`, and an `&` becomes `%26`. In a query string, a space can also be written as `+`, which is why the search above says `red+shoes`.

You'll see `%20` in the address of any file with a space in its name: a picture saved as `my photo.png` is at `my%20photo.png`. That's one reason web developers name their files in lowercase, with dashes in place of spaces, like `my-photo.png`.

steps.title: Paths: finding a file in a folder
steps.body:
Every link, picture, and stylesheet on a page points at a file by its path. A path that's off by one letter or one folder is the most common reason a picture doesn't show or a page comes up without its styles, so this part is worth reading slowly.

## The path walks through folders

On a site made of files, the path is the route through the site's folders to one file. It starts at the site's main folder, called the **root** and written as a lone `/`. Each `/` after that steps into a folder, and the last piece is the file.

```diagram site-paths
The path is the file's place in the folder, starting from the root.
```

So `/about.html` is the file `about.html` in the main folder, and `/images/logo.png` is `logo.png` inside the `images` folder. The server takes the path from the request, finds that spot in its folder, and sends the file it finds there.

## The home page

A path that ends at a folder, like `/` or `/images/`, doesn't name a file. For these, servers look for a file called `index.html` in that folder and send it. That's why the home page is called `index.html`: asking for `https://example.com/` gets you the `index.html` in the root folder.

## When the path is wrong

When there's no file at the path, the server answers `404 Not Found`. These slips cause most of them:

- **A letter's case.** Most servers treat `About.html` and `about.html` as two different files, even when your own computer doesn't. Keep file names lowercase.
- **A missing folder.** `/logo.png` and `/images/logo.png` are different places.
- **The wrong extension.** `logo.jpg` won't find a file called `logo.png`.

## Paths that aren't files

A server that generates its answers can treat a path however it likes. The `/search` in the previous part isn't a file anywhere: a program reads the path and the query string, and builds a page of results. Shops use paths like `/products/42` for product number 42, with no file of that name. You can't tell from the address which kind you're looking at, and you don't need to, since the browser asks the same way either way.

## Shorter paths inside a page

When you write a link inside a page, you rarely type the whole address. A **relative** path leaves out the start of the address, and the browser fills it in from the page it's on. A full address, with a scheme and a host, is called **absolute**.

Here's how the browser fills in four links on the page `https://example.com/blog/first-post.html`, a file in the `blog` folder. Each one ends up on `example.com`, at the path shown:

- `second-post.html` goes to `/blog/second-post.html`, a file next to this page, in the same folder.
- `images/cat.jpg` goes to `/blog/images/cat.jpg`, inside a folder next to this page.
- `../about.html` goes to `/about.html`, since `..` means up one folder.
- `/about.html` goes to `/about.html` too, since a path that starts with `/` starts at the root.

Relative paths are why a whole site can move to a new domain name and keep working: none of its links mention the old one. The HTML lessons come back to links and show when to use each kind.

steps.title: Try it: a server on your computer
steps.body:
Reading about servers only goes so far. Running one and watching each request arrive makes the last four parts real, and it's how you'll work on every site in this course: you build it on your own computer first, and look at it in your browser as you go. ## Make a tiny site Open the Playground with the **Playground** button at the top of this lesson. In its Explorer, make a folder called `my-site`, and in it two files: right-click the folder, choose to make a new file, type its name, and paste in its text. Name the first one `index.html`, the home page: ```html My site

Welcome to my site

About me

``` Name the second one `about.html`. It's the page from the first part of this lesson: ```html About me

About me

I am learning how the web works.

``` The `` tag on the home page makes a link, and its `href` holds where the link goes. `about.html` is a relative path, so it means the file next to this page. ## Start a server Your computer can run a server too. **Python**, a programming language, comes with a small one built in, which sends the files in whatever folder you start it from. On a Mac, Python came with the developer tools installed along with Hack University. The first example below shows the two commands to type in the Playground's terminal, and what they printed. The first command, `cd my-site`, moves the terminal into the folder. `cd` stands for change directory, and the server sends the files of the folder the terminal is in. In the second command, `8000` is the port the server listens on, and `--bind 127.0.0.1` keeps the server private to your computer, so nobody else on your Wi-Fi can reach it. The next lesson explains both. On Windows, if the terminal says it can't find `python3`, type this in place of the second command: ```bash npx http-server -a 127.0.0.1 -p 8000 ``` `npx` came with Node.js, and it downloads a small server program and runs it, on the same port and just as private. If it asks to install `http-server`, type `y` and press Enter. It prints different messages from the ones below, but it works the same way. The server prints one line and then waits. The terminal stays busy while it runs, and that's normal: it's listening for requests. When you're done, press **Ctrl+C** in the terminal to stop it. ## Visit it Open a new browser tab and go to `http://localhost:8000/`. **localhost** is a name that always means this same computer, so the browser asks the server you just started. You'll see Welcome to my site: the `index.html` in your folder. Then: 1. Click **About me**. The browser asks for `/about.html` and shows it. 2. Go to `http://localhost:8000/contact.html`, a file that doesn't exist. The browser shows the server's Error response page, with error code 404. 3. Go to `http://localhost:8000/about.html#hobbies`, the same page with a fragment on the end. Each time the browser asks for something, the server prints a line in the terminal. Your browser may also ask for `/favicon.ico` without being told to. That's the little picture on a browser tab, and browsers look for one on every site, so a 404 for it is harmless. ## See the whole response Your browser shows you the page, but not the response it came in. `curl` shows you all of it. The Playground's terminal is busy running the server, so use your computer's own terminal for this (Terminal on a Mac, Command Prompt on Windows), as the second example shows.

examples.title: Starting the server, then visiting it
examples.prompt: In the Playground's terminal, go into the folder and start the server. Then follow the three steps above in your browser. This is everything the terminal printed.
examples.explanation: The first line is the server saying it's ready: it's serving on `127.0.0.1`, the number that localhost stands for, at port 8000. Each line after that is one request, and they all read the same way. `127.0.0.1` is who asked: your own computer. The square brackets hold when. Then comes the request itself, in quotes: `GET`, the path, and `HTTP/1.1`, the version of the rules the browser used. The number after it is the status code the server answered with. The first visit asked for `/` and got 200, with `index.html`. The click asked for `/about.html`. The missing page got 404, with an extra line saying why. In the last line, the server got `/about.html` with no `#hobbies`, since the fragment never leaves the browser. It answered 304 instead of 200: the browser still had a copy from the click, so it asked whether the file had changed, and 304 means it hasn't, so use the copy you have.

examples.title: The whole response, as curl sees it
examples.prompt: With the server still running, ask it for the about page from a second terminal. The `-i` tells curl to show the start of the response too, not only the file.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.0 200 OK Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.13.6 Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 20:19:24 GMT Content-type: text/html Content-Length: 98 Last-Modified: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 20:07:14 GMT About me

About me

I am learning how the web works.
examples.explanation: The first line is the **status line**: `200 OK`, so the server found the file. `HTTP/1.0` is the version of the rules Python's server uses, older than the browser's, which is fine on your own computer. The lines after it are **headers**: facts about the response, one per line, each a name and a value. `Server` names the server program, `Date` is when it answered, `Content-type: text/html` tells the browser the file is a page, `Content-Length: 98` says how many bytes follow, and `Last-Modified` is when the file last changed. After a blank line comes the file itself, the same 98 bytes that are in your folder. Ask again and you'll get the same bytes, because it's a static response. The next lesson reads every piece of messages like this one.

recap:
- A website is a folder of files, mostly HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and pictures, kept on a computer that stays on.
- A server is the program that sends those files, and your browser is a client that asks for them.
- A request asks for one thing by its path, and a response answers with a status code, like 200 or 404, and the thing itself.
- A static response is a file sent as it is, and a generated one is made by a program at the moment you ask.
- A URL has a scheme, a host, a path, a query string, and a fragment, and the fragment never reaches the server.
- A path walks from the site's root folder to one file, and a path that ends at a folder gets that folder's index.html.
- localhost always means your own computer, so a server you start there is yours to try things on.
